intro: Business analyst SQL query performance optimization is the essential process of refining code to ensure your database requests run efficiently. When your queries hang or time out, it prevents you from delivering the insights your team needs to make informed decisions.
tldr: Use the EXPLAIN command to see how your database handles your query.
Stop using SELECT * and only retrieve the columns you actually require.
Filter your data as early as possible to keep your result sets small.
Keep your database statistics current to help the query optimizer work correctly.

blocks.text: Why SQL query performance matters for business analysts

As a business analyst, your work depends on timely access to data. When you run a query that takes minutes instead of seconds, your workflow stops. You cannot perform analysis, build your pivot tables, or update your dashboards while waiting for the server.

Inefficient queries also place unnecessary strain on your company infrastructure. A poorly written query can trigger a full table scan, reading millions of rows when it only needs ten. This consumes server memory and CPU, which can slow down the entire database for your colleagues.
Common causes of slow SQL queries

items: Retrieving too much data by using SELECT * instead of specifying columns.
Missing indexes on columns used in WHERE clauses or JOIN conditions.
Performing joins on columns with different data types, forcing the database to convert values.
Outdated database statistics that lead the optimizer to choose a sub-optimal execution plan.
Using functions on indexed columns in the WHERE clause, which prevents the database from using the index.

blocks.text: How to fix SQL performance without paid tools

You do not need expensive software to start optimizing. Begin by running EXPLAIN before your query. This command shows you the execution plan. It tells you if the database is doing a full table scan or using an index. Look for high-cost operations in the output.

Next, be specific with your SELECT statements. If you only need three columns, list them explicitly. This reduces the amount of data transferred from the database server to your Mac. It also lowers the memory footprint of your query.

Finally, check your indexes. If you filter by date, ensure the date column is indexed. Use the ANALYZE command regularly to update your database statistics. This ensures the query optimizer has the most accurate information to make decisions.

causes.title: Full table scans
causes.text: The database reads every row instead of using an index to find the data.

causes.title: Excessive data retrieval
causes.text: Using SELECT * pulls back far more information than you actually need for your report.

fixes.title: Use EXPLAIN
fixes.text: Run EXPLAIN before your query to understand the execution path.

fixes.title: Limit columns
fixes.text: Only select the columns that are necessary for your analysis.

fixes.title: Update statistics
fixes.text: Run ANALYZE to ensure the database optimizer has current data.
